title: More Collaboration, Slower System: Counterintuitive Management from the Product Chiefs at Snap and Discord
dek: Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately internalizes collaboration costs aggressively, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.
why: High information density, but the back half is worth more than the front half. For people who want to hear how a product leader actually makes decisions, not for people who want specific growth playbooks.
who: Product leaders, startup founders, engineering and design managers currently wrestling with collaboration and decision-making efficiency.
skip: The opening intro and the Ustream reminiscences can be skipped; the ad mechanics and management principles in the middle and back half are the most valuable.

points.h: More collaboration makes the system slower
points.body: Peter says you will never hear an executive say ‘stop collaborating,’ and to him that is precisely a warning sign. Collaboration brings enormous coordination costs, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So he deliberately and aggressively internalizes collaboration costs, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better. This is also where his ‘design teams like a terrorist organization’ comes from: one ideological culture that makes everyone understand why we are doing this, plus a very clear organizational structure specifying who can be trusted with which decision. With those two things, you don't need to over-collaborate and you still get results that feel like you collaborated.

points.h: The median PM gap is a math-structure problem
points.body: Peter offers a distributional explanation: product management ability is normally distributed in the population, and the people who actually become PMs are cut from the right tail; once you cut it, it becomes a power-law distribution, and the median of a power law is far below the mean. Layer on two more mechanisms: in the ZERP era it became the most lucrative career in tech for people without a technical background, and the definition is subjective, so the people who get in have extremely strong incentives to stay; meanwhile the genuinely strong ones have skills that map almost perfectly onto other executive roles or starting their own company, so ‘great product managers are exiting the system.’ Squeezed from both ends, the median is naturally bad. He also points out that the people actually complaining about PMs are the middle cohort of engineers — great engineers know how to bend a PM into the shape they want, and terrible engineers can hide behind the PM's decisions.

points.h: Snap's ads can't scale for three mathematical reasons
points.body: First, the users are extremely young, and between 17 and 18, and between 18 and 21, there is a ‘suspicious discontinuity’ in ad CPMs in and outside the US; the rules for tracking, measuring and targeting under-17s are extremely strict, and what is hard to measure is hard to build performance products around. Second, almost all non-search display advertising runs on a screen that exists to show ads, whereas Snap opens a camera — in the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to a friend, there is no logical place to put an ad; it is a creation-oriented product, not a consumption-oriented one. Third, it is fundamentally a messaging app, and there is currently no good messaging ad product; Asian chat apps get cited over and over, but break it down by dollars spent per unit of time and none of them does particularly well.

points.h: Taste is the nerve to leave good things on the shelf
points.body: Peter says one thing he learned at Snap: he watched Evan say no to better ideas than almost anything any other consumer startup has ever shipped. He describes the product leader's goal as turning the founder into the world's richest museum curator — what is on display in the product right now is only a small fraction of the whole collection, the pieces the curator judged right for this time and place. He offers a way to probe taste in interviews: ask what the person built but never shipped — not something killed because the data was bad, but a prototype they held in their hands and then judged ‘the world isn't ready’ or ‘this thing isn't ready.’ If a museum hung its entire collection on the walls, the curator would have done nothing.

points.h: Advertising is the internet's product-market fit
points.body: Peter comes down squarely on Eric Seufert's side: advertising is the internet's product-market fit, and subscription consumer products are overrated. He judges OpenAI to have ‘last mover advantage’ in ads — Meta already solved modern ad auctions, this ‘solved problem,’ from 2010 to 2020, and OpenAI is just running through each component fast. Mechanically he names the modified VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) auction: the highest bidder doesn't win; instead the advertiser's natural value for that user is folded into the bid, so a high bidder who wants to reach people who don't want to be reached has to pay more. This mechanism lets organic and ad content sit in the same auction, with dollars as the common denominator.

points.h: In chat, the denominator for ads is trust, not relevance
points.body: Peter replaces ‘natural value’ in VCG with ‘trust’ in the chat context. A user asks ‘which microphone should I buy,’ and the product has to decide whether to give an objective answer, a set of answers, or an advertiser-influenced one — and the degree of influence should equal how much trust you are willing to trade away. He uses Amazon search as an example: search for something and you scroll past 16 ads before the first real result, which subtly erodes users' trust in the system. So OpenAI's real deciding factor is not whether to do ads, but how to mathematically maximize long-term trust inside the auction mechanism — trust maximization is probably correlated with retention, and may even be causal.

points.h: Growth comes from the core, not from new markets
points.body: Verified twice, at Snap and Discord: a network-effects business already wants to grow, and the most effective move is to serve the people already using it, or wanting to use it for its actual job, better — faster, more relevant. He explains with eighth-grade math: it takes 30 monthly actives to equal one daily active, so consumer products should optimize the DAU/MAU ratio; moving that ratio a few basis points is far more worthwhile than pulling in a pile of new MAUs and gambling on retention. Snap's lesson came from the disastrous 2018 redesign, the only quarter Snap's overall DAU went flat quarter over quarter; after that the team ground away at Android performance, producing a multi-year growth revival. Discord's version is more counterintuitive: at the time Midjourney was built on Discord and everyone outside thought this was Discord's big opportunity, but Peter says if you pull up the Discord usage curve, you simply cannot pick out the Midjourney stretch.

points.h: SpaceX is burning its own ships
points.body: Peter considers SpaceX the greatest company right now, and the most instructive thing is how it fights the future: Falcon 9 is the world's best reusable launch system, other countries would trade GDP for it, and SpaceX announced it will stop selling Falcon 9 seats in a few years and move to Starship. He calls this a Cortez-level burning of the ships, a way to avoid what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma — because even holding the best thing, you are still willing to build the thing that makes your current product irrelevant. He also notes that SpaceX and Tesla publish ten-year plans on their websites, and Tesla even open-sources its patents; that confidence — ‘I'll tell you what to do, and if you think you can do it better, come copy it’ — is what he aspires to as a product leader.

points.h: Long-term greedy: using ideology as cover for long-termism
points.body: The phrase Peter used over and over on the ad teams at Snap and Discord is long-term greedy. Behind it is math: tomorrow's ad revenue is causally linked to the ROI you create for advertisers today, so the focus should be on advertiser ROI. The hard part is that the easiest way to improve ROI is to lower the denominator — just cut prices — and in a modern auction price is an output, not an input. What he really means is: every career has moments when long-termism is excruciating, like a public company missing its numbers and possibly having to lay people off, and at those moments you need an ideology as ‘cover’ that gives you room to make long-term decisions — we are not doing charity, we are giving up margin today because we know they will come back tomorrow with a bigger budget.

points.h: Core product value takes seven years of weekly repetition
points.body: Peter says Snap's core product value was not a slogan on a wall but an onboarding presentation he personally gave to every new hire, weekly or every other week, for seven straight years. His logic: with metrics but no story, data scientists and engineers won't act on it every day; with a story but no metrics, nobody knows what to optimize. So you need both, and you need to repeat it — part of what he calls the ‘cult’: this is how we deliver core product value, this is why people still choose Snapchat every day against a sea of alternatives and a pack of ferocious competitors.

points.h: A great PM is three pairs of fighting wolves
points.body: Peter thinks great PM is itself an oxymoron, specifically three contradictions: first, extreme confidence bordering on arrogance, alongside genuinely serious humility that accurately credits the designer who changed the design at the last second and the engineer who pulled an all-nighter for a partner event; second, extremely organized and respectful of process, while also extremely tolerant of ambiguity and almost pathologically allergic to authority — ‘I have a checklist for everything, but I can also throw it out and redo it at any moment’; third, long-term thinking coexisting with an almost annoying bias to action, where a good PM sets the cadence for the whole company — ‘he wakes up in the morning and the team is awake.’

points.h: Some consumer product ability cannot be learned
points.body: Peter's spiciest point: to build truly great consumer products for certain specific populations, the PMs and designers on those products need certain non-negotiable traits that cannot be learned or acquired — he explicitly lists gender, race, ethnicity and socioeconomic background. He stresses this is not the simple mapping of ‘building a product for young Black men, so hire young Black men,’ but rather that most consumer products are essentially playing to certain parts of Maslow's hierarchy, and people with certain upbringings and physical conditions understand those needs better. He also admits this is in many cases not even executable, which is exactly why it is the spicy take.
